svg.title: How a damping ring makes a beam narrower
svg.desc: Drawing in five scenes, one under the other. 1 A ring of pipe seen at an angle, with five blue bending magnets, a grey cavity and a short wiggler. A wide, fuzzy beam of particles joins it at the upper left, runs round it clockwise for thousands of turns, and a thin beam leaves it at the lower left. 2 A close view of one end of the ring, where three magnets bend the path and copper coloured light flies off forwards at each of them. 3 A close view of the cavity, a row of rounded metal cells on the pipe, with arrows that show its push forwards along the beam. 4 Two beams compared. The beam that goes in is a wide, untidy cloud of particles and the beam that comes out thousands of turns later is a thin, sharp line. 5 On a dark panel, a close view of the wiggler. Two rows of magnet blocks, one above the beam and one below, with north and south poles alternating along each row and opposite poles facing each other. Between the rows lies a flat sheet, and on it the beam follows a wave from side to side, drawn exaggerated. A bright point marks every bend, and copper coloured light leaves each one forwards. In the EPITA project these magnets are permanent and need no electric current.
